title: GC Algorithms & Tuning
scopeHtml: Generational hypothesis, Serial/Parallel/G1/ZGC/Shenandoah, G1 internals, concurrent collector design, collector choice, key flags and defaults per version, heap/young sizing, promotion failures, reading GC logs.

questions.promptHtml: What is the generational hypothesis, and why do most JVM garbage collectors split the heap into young and old generations?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every GC tuning conversation rests on this. It separates people who memorized collector names from people who know why GC costs what it costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The weak generational hypothesis says most objects die young and few young objects are referenced by old ones. So I collect the small young region often and cheaply, copying the few survivors out, and touch the big old region rarely. GC cost is proportional to live data, not garbage, so scanning a mostly-dead young region is a huge win."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A tracing collector's cost is proportional to the live objects it must trace or copy, not to the garbage. If 98% of a 200 MB young region is dead, a copying collector moves only ~4 MB and frees the rest at once; there is no per-dead-object work.

 allocation -> [Eden] --minor GC--> [Survivor S0/S1] --age >= threshold--> [Old]
                 ^ ~95%+ dies here     ^ copied between survivors        ^ collected rarely

Pieces that make it work:

  • Bump-pointer allocation in Eden (and TLABs per thread) makes allocation a few instructions.
  • Copying young collection compacts for free (survivors become contiguous).
  • Tenuring: survivors age by one per young GC; at the tenuring threshold (max 15, adapted by -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold; verify default per collector) they move to old.
  • Old to young references are the catch: a young GC must treat them as roots without scanning old. A card table / remembered set (maintained by a write barrier) records which old regions hold such pointers.

When the hypothesis fails (large caches, sessions, big batch results that live a long time but not forever), objects get copied several times and then promoted, and old fills with medium-lived garbage, forcing expensive old collections. That is the workload shape that makes "just add heap" not work.

Not every modern collector is generational: ZGC was single-generation until Generational ZGC (JDK 21 opt-in, default in 23); Shenandoah is single-generation by default, generational mode is a product feature in JDK 25 (verified on openjdk.org JEPs 439/474/521 and the Shenandoah wiki).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Typical request path: almost everything here dies before the next young GC
List<Dto> rows = repo.findAll();           // short-lived
String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(rows); // short-lived
// A static cache keeps things alive for hours: this is what stresses old gen
static final Map<String, Dto> CACHE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "young GC is fast because young is small". It is fast because survivors are few; a young GC with lots of survivors is slow.
  • Believing garbage volume makes GC slower. Allocation rate affects GC frequency; live set affects GC duration.
  • Forgetting the old-to-young pointer problem (card marking) has a real write-barrier cost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why copying and not mark-sweep in young? → Dead objects cost nothing, compaction is free, allocation stays bump-pointer.
  2. What is premature promotion? → Survivor space too small or objects too big, so short-lived objects get tenured and become old-gen garbage.
  3. How can a young GC be slow if young is small? → Many survivors, large remembered-set/root scanning (big old gen with many dirty cards), or too few GC threads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "new objects in young, old ones in old." Senior: ties cost to live set, explains remembered sets as the price of generations, and names workloads (big long-lived caches, ZGC/Shenandoah pre-generational) where the hypothesis does or does not pay.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service holding a 6 GB in-heap cache with 30-minute TTL churned entries through young survivors into old, producing constant mixed GCs. Moving the cache off-heap/external cut GC CPU from 18% to 4% (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: Name the HotSpot garbage collectors and when you would pick each. Which one is the default, and does that depend on the Java version or the machine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the landscape and the defaults that silently decide your production behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Serial is single-threaded for tiny heaps and containers with one CPU. Parallel maximizes throughput with stop-the-world multi-threaded collections. G1 is the default since Java 9 on server-class machines and balances pause and throughput by region. ZGC and Shenandoah are low-pause concurrent collectors for latency-sensitive or large heaps. Java 8 defaulted to Parallel. And if the JVM sees fewer than 2 CPUs or too little memory, it falls back to Serial even on Java 17 or 21."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Collector Flag Pause behavior Best for
Serial -XX:+UseSerialGC STW, single thread Small heaps (<~100-200 MB), 1 CPU, CLI tools
Parallel -XX:+UseParallelGC STW, N threads, longest pauses on big heaps Batch jobs, throughput over latency
G1 -XX:+UseG1GC STW young/mixed, concurrent marking, target pause General services, 4-64 GB heaps
ZGC -XX:+UseZGC Concurrent; STW phases sub-millisecond-class Latency-critical, very large heaps
Shenandoah -XX:+UseShenandoahGC Concurrent evacuation Low pause; in Red Hat/Corretto/Zulu etc., Oracle does not ship it

Defaults:

  • JDK 8: Parallel. JDK 9+: G1 if the machine is "server-class" (docs: at least 2 CPUs and roughly 2 GB; verify the exact threshold in -Xlog:gc+init or java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version). Otherwise Serial.
  • In containers the JVM reads cgroup limits, so a pod with cpu: 500m (rounds to 1 CPU) silently gets Serial.
  • CMS was deprecated in 9 and removed in 14. ZGC went production in 15. Generational ZGC: -XX:+ZGenerational in 21, default in 23 (JEP 474). Generational Shenandoah is a product feature in 25 (JEP 521).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -Xlog:gc+init -version                 # prints which collector and CPU/heap ergonomics
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "Use(Serial|Parallel|G1|Z|Shenandoah)GC"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming G1 everywhere. Small container => Serial.
  • Mixing legacy flags (-XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC fails on 14+).
  • Picking ZGC "because it's newest" for a throughput batch job.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you check which GC is running? → jcmd <pid> VM.info, -Xlog:gc+init, or jinfo -flag UseG1GC.
  2. Why might a 2-core pod run Serial? → Ergonomics: fewer than 2 available processors or too little memory classifies it as non-server.
  3. Why does Oracle JDK not have Shenandoah? → It is a Red Hat-led project; availability is per vendor build (per the Shenandoah wiki).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists names. Senior states per-version defaults, the container fallback to Serial, and picks by pause/throughput/footprint trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kubernetes migration cut the CPU limit to 1; pauses went from 60 ms to 900 ms because the JVM quietly switched from G1 to Serial.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what happens during a young (minor) GC. What are Eden, survivor spaces and tenuring?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The base mechanism for every later tuning discussion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Threads allocate into Eden via TLABs. When Eden is full, the JVM stops the world, finds live objects from roots plus the remembered set of old-to-young pointers, and copies them to a survivor space or promotes them to old if old enough. Eden and the other survivor are then empty. Survivors age by one each cycle until the tenuring threshold."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Allocation: each thread has a TLAB (thread-local allocation buffer) in Eden; bump pointer, no locking.
  2. Eden full -> safepoint -> GC threads start from roots (thread stacks, statics, JNI, plus dirty cards from old gen).
  3. Live objects copied to the to survivor (or old if age >= threshold, or survivor overflow).
  4. Eden and from survivor are wiped logically (pointer reset). Roles of survivor spaces swap.
Before: Eden[ABCDE...full] S0[x y] S1[ ]
After : Eden[ ]            S0[ ]   S1[A C x y]   (age +1)   B,D,E dead -> no cost
  • Pause = f(survivor volume + root/card scanning), not Eden size.
  • Overflow: if survivors do not fit the survivor space, objects are promoted early (premature promotion) and old fills with short-lived garbage.
  • Dynamic threshold: adaptive tenuring (-XX:+UseAdaptiveSizePolicy in Parallel, TargetSurvivorRatio default 50 in Serial/Parallel; verify per collector) lowers the age if survivor space would exceed the target occupancy. In G1, survivor sizing is set dynamically by the pause model.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -Xlog:gc*,gc+age=trace:file=gc.log:time,uptime ...
# gc+age=trace shows the age table: how many bytes survive at each age

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking Eden is "cleaned" by sweeping. It is reset after copying.
  • Sizing Eden huge to reduce frequency while ignoring that a larger Eden with a burst of survivors yields a longer pause.
  • Ignoring humongous and TLAB-bypassing large allocations that skip Eden logic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a TLAB and why does it matter? → Per-thread allocation buffer; lock-free bump allocation; large objects fall out of it.
  2. What happens if old gen is full during promotion? → Promotion failure; falls back to Full GC (stop-the-world, slow).
  3. Why two survivor spaces? → Copy source and target without fragmentation; one always empty.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can describe Eden/Survivor/Old. Senior says pause scales with survivors and card scanning, and reads the age table to tune tenuring.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A batch exporter built large Lists in Eden; each young GC copied 800 MB of survivors. Streaming the output made young pauses drop from 250 ms to 15 ms (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml:
Read this G1 log and tell me what happened. How do you enable GC logging in modern Java?

[12.401s][info][gc] GC(41) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 3584M->412M(8192M) 22.318ms
[98.220s][info][gc] GC(97) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 5100M->3900M(8192M) 31.002ms
[98.231s][info][gc] GC(98) Concurrent Mark Cycle
[103.870s][info][gc] GC(98) Pause Remark 4300M->3800M(8192M) 18.4ms
[104.600s][info][gc] GC(99) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 4100M->3000M(8192M) 61.7ms

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every GC investigation starts with the log. Few candidates read one fluently.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Format is before->after(committed) then pause. Line 1 is a routine young GC: 3.5 GB to 412 MB in 22 ms. Line 2 is a young GC that also started concurrent marking, triggered by a humongous allocation, with heap at about 62% of capacity. Then Remark ends marking, and the Mixed GC starts reclaiming old regions at 62 ms. Logging is unified -Xlog since Java 9."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Parse each field: GC(n) id, cause in parentheses, used before -> used after (current committed heap), then wall-clock pause.

  • Line 1: Eden freed ~3.1 GB, survivors/promotions leave 412 MB. Healthy.
  • Line 2: "Concurrent Start" means G1 began marking old gen. Cause "G1 Humongous Allocation" means a humongous request pushed occupancy past IHOP (adaptive, initially 45%): 3900/8192 = 47.6% post-GC, consistent.
  • Line 3-4: Marking runs concurrently with the app; Remark is a short STW finishing marking.
  • Line 5: Mixed collection: young + selected old regions. Heap goes 4100M -> 3000M.

What to scan for: Pause Full (bad), To-space exhausted / Evacuation Failure, Humongous causes, pause trend vs MaxGCPauseMillis, Concurrent Mark Cycle that starts too late (look for Full GC right after).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Java 9+
java -Xlog:gc*,gc+heap=debug:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20M -jar app.jar
# Java 8 (legacy flags)
java -XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps -Xloggc:gc.log -jar app.jar

Analyze with GCeasy, GCViewer, or JFR's GC events.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Logging only in prod after an incident; keep it on always (low overhead, rotate files).
  • Confusing "pause" in the log with request latency; the pause is only STW time, queued requests add to it.
  • Comparing used to Xmx, ignoring committed heap and off-heap.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Pause Full (Allocation Failure) imply? → Concurrent cycle lost the race or fragmentation/humongous; tune IHOP or fix allocation.
  2. How do you see per-phase breakdown? → -Xlog:gc+phases=debug.
  3. Where else do you see GC info live? → JFR GC events, jstat -gcutil, Micrometer jvm.gc.pause.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE reads pause times. Senior infers causes (IHOP crossing, humongous trigger), checks trend and what happens after concurrent mark, and correlates with request latency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team found p99 spikes only in the gc+phases output: 40 ms of "Ext Root Scanning" due to thousands of threads (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: Explain how G1 organizes the heap and what the collection set is. Why is it called "Garbage First"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: G1 is the production default; this is the baseline for every tuning answer.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "G1 splits the heap into equal regions, 1 to 32 MB, each dynamically assigned a role: Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous. A collection picks a set of regions, the collection set, that it can evacuate within the pause target. 'Garbage first' means that for old regions it prefers the ones with the most reclaimable space, because they give the most free memory per unit of copying work."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Region size is chosen from the initial/max heap, a power of two between 1 and 32 MB aiming at about 2048 regions (-XX:G1HeapRegionSize to override; verify the target ratio per version). Heap of 8 GB => 4 MB regions.
  • No fixed contiguous young/old. Young size is a set of regions, adjusted each cycle by a pause-time predictor to meet -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms), bounded by G1NewSizePercent (default 5) and G1MaxNewSizePercent (default 60) of the heap, per the G1 docs (verify values per version).
  • Cycle (from the Oracle tuning guide): young-only phase (young GCs, and when old occupancy crosses IHOP a Concurrent Start piggybacks marking on a young GC, then Remark and Cleanup) -> space-reclamation phase (Mixed GCs) -> back to young-only.
  • Per-region remembered sets track incoming pointers so any subset of regions can be evacuated independently. That is the enabling structure, and its cost is memory (typically a few percent to 20% of heap; verify) and write-barrier overhead.
  • Evacuation: live objects copy to new regions, source regions freed, heap compacts incrementally. No separate permanent old/young compaction.
| E | E | O | O | S | H | H | H | O | free | E | O |   E=eden S=survivor O=old H=humongous
   collection set chosen by predicted cost <= pause goal; old picks sorted by garbage ratio

sections.label: Code
sections.html: java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms8g -Xmx8g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=150 -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m -Xlog:gc* -jar app.jar

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling the pause target a guarantee. It is a goal, "with high probability", not real-time.
  • Setting -Xmn or NewRatio with G1: this disables the adaptive young sizing that G1 relies on to meet the goal.
  • Thinking G1 has fixed 5%-style young generation; it floats.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a remembered set in G1? → Per-region record of incoming references from other regions; lets regions be collected independently.
  2. Why can pauses exceed the goal? → Too many survivors, large remembered sets, evacuation failure, low CPU.
  3. What does Full GC do in G1? → Parallel stop-the-world compacting of the whole heap since JDK 10 (JEP 307); still the worst case.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "regions, pause goal." Senior: the collection set is chosen by a cost model, young floats within bounds, remembered sets are the memory cost, and manual young sizing defeats the model.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team pinned -Xmn2g on G1 after a G1 migration and got 600 ms pauses under bursts; removing it restored predictable behavior (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: How does G1 decide when to start concurrent marking and how does it reclaim old regions? What is IHOP and what goes wrong if marking starts too late?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The G1 failure mode in real production is "marking lost the race, Full GC". This probes whether you understand the race.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "G1 starts concurrent marking when old-gen occupancy crosses the Initiating Heap Occupancy Percent, which is 45% initially and adaptive by default. After marking and cleanup, it runs several mixed GCs that add the most garbage-heavy old regions to each young collection. If the old gen fills before marking and mixed GCs finish, G1 hits to-space exhaustion or a full GC."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Phases:

  1. Concurrent Start (STW, piggybacked on a young GC): snapshot roots. Uses SATB (snapshot-at-the-beginning): the write barrier logs overwritten references so objects live at the snapshot are never missed.
  2. Concurrent Mark: traverse the heap concurrently with the app.
  3. Remark (STW, short): finish SATB buffers, reference processing.
  4. Cleanup: reclaim fully empty regions, pick candidate old regions.
  5. Mixed GCs: roughly G1MixedGCCountTarget (default 8) collections; each takes young plus some old candidates. Candidates with reclaimable space below G1HeapWastePercent (default 5) are skipped, and mixed GCs stop when waste is below that.

IHOP: with G1UseAdaptiveIHOP (default true), G1 measures allocation rate and marking time and starts early enough to finish before old is full; the flag value 45 is only the initial value. If you disable adaptive IHOP, 45 is static and a high promotion rate will lose the race.

The race: time to mark + time for mixed GCs must be less than time for allocation/promotion to fill the remaining free space. G1ReservePercent (default 10) holds free space back as headroom to reduce evacuation failures.

Symptoms of losing: Pause Young (Concurrent Start) followed by to-space exhausted, then Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=35 -XX:-G1UseAdaptiveIHOP   # static, earlier marking (a hammer)
-XX:G1ReservePercent=15 -XX:ConcGCThreads=4                    # more headroom, faster marking

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Lowering IHOP blindly: marking constantly, wasting CPU.
  • Raising MaxGCPauseMillis to fix Full GCs; the cause is the race, not the goal.
  • Assuming mixed GCs are always short; each one adds old-region evacuation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is SATB? → Marking from a logical snapshot; the barrier records deleted references so nothing live is lost.
  2. What does ConcGCThreads do? → Threads for concurrent marking; default derives from ParallelGCThreads (about a quarter; verify).
  3. Where does a large Humongous Allocation fit? → It can trigger a Concurrent Start directly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "G1 does mixed GCs." Senior frames it as a race between marking+reclaim and allocation, names adaptive IHOP, SATB, reserve and the evidence in logs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Ingestion service at 400 MB/s promotion rate: static IHOP of 45% was too late on a 12 GB heap; fix was adaptive IHOP plus more concurrent threads (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: What is a humongous object in G1, why is it a problem, and how do you find and fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Humongous allocation is the classic hidden G1 killer (large arrays, buffers, JSON blobs).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A humongous object is one at least half a region. G1 allocates it directly into contiguous old-type regions, bypassing Eden. It wastes the unused tail of its last region, can fragment the heap, triggers concurrent cycles early, and historically was only freed by marking or eager reclaim. I find them with GC logs and JFR allocation events, then fix by streaming, chunking, or raising region size."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Threshold: size >= region/2. Region 4 MB => objects >= 2 MB are humongous (G1 docs).
  • Humongous objects start at a region boundary; the last region's tail is unusable. A 2.1 MB array in 4 MB regions occupies one region (1.9 MB wasted, ~47%); a 4.1 MB array takes two regions (3.9 MB wasted).
  • They need contiguous free regions: after fragmentation, a request can fail even with enough total free space and force a Full GC.
  • Eager reclaim (G1EagerReclaimHumongousObjects, enabled by default): humongous objects of primitive arrays with no incoming references can be freed at a young GC without waiting for marking; works for byte[]/int[], not reference arrays.
  • Allocation of humongous objects counts toward IHOP and can trigger the Concurrent Start cause G1 Humongous Allocation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: reading a whole 50 MB file into byte[] on every request
byte[] all = Files.readAllBytes(path);

// Better: stream in 64 KB chunks
try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(path)) {
    in.transferTo(response.getOutputStream());
}
-Xlog:gc+humongous=debug          # humongous allocation sizes/regions
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m          # raises threshold to 8 MB; costs coarser granularity
jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB rec.jfr   # stack of big allocs

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Raising region size as the only fix; you move the threshold but keep a bad pattern.
  • Forgetting growing ArrayList/StringBuilder/ByteArrayOutputStream backing arrays cross the threshold silently.
  • Forgetting ByteBuf/byte[] pools in clients.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Max region size? → 32 MB, so humongous at 16 MB+ (verify).
  2. Why is Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) repeating? → Allocation spikes keep pushing occupancy over IHOP.
  3. Does ZGC have humongous objects? → No; ZGC uses small/medium/large page classes with different cost profile.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "avoid big arrays." Senior computes waste per region size, knows the contiguity and eager-reclaim details, and finds the stack with JFR.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A CSV export built a 120 MB byte[] per request; three concurrent exports produced Full GCs despite 60% free heap because no contiguous run was available (illustrative).

questions.contextHtml:
A payments API (Java 17, 8 CPU / 16 GB container, 4 GB heap wanted) was migrated from Java 8 Parallel GC. The team carried over its flags. After rollout, p99 rose from 120 ms to 480 ms, and GC logs show a Young pause every ~300 ms and occasional Pause Full.

JAVA_OPTS="-XX:+UseG1GC -Xms512m -Xmx4g -Xmn3g -XX:SurvivorRatio=6 \
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=5 -XX:ParallelGCThreads=2 \
  -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC -XX:+DisableExplicitGC"
questions.promptHtml: Review these flags. What is wrong, what would you change, and what would you keep?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise MaxGCPauseMillis a bit." It misses that the JVM may not even start (CMS flag), and that -Xmn/SurvivorRatio disable G1's adaptive model.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the real SLOs (p99 target)? Allocation rate and live set? Is the heap growing at runtime (why Xms != Xmx)? Does any library use NIO direct buffers or call System.gc() (why DisableExplicitGC)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to the known-good flag set or drop the suspicious flags first, since the config is the only change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) -Xmn3g fixes young at 3 GB out of 4 GB, leaving ~1 GB old and no room for mixed GCs: Full GCs. (b) MaxGCPauseMillis=5 is unachievable, so G1 shrinks young to the minimum (G1NewSizePercent, 5%), giving frequent GCs (every 300 ms) and high GC CPU. (c) ParallelGCThreads=2 on 8 CPUs makes each STW slower. (d) UseConcMarkSweepGC was removed in JDK 14; on 17 the JVM exits with "Unrecognized VM option" unless -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions is set, so check the actual launch flags. (e) Xms << Xmx causes heap resizing churn.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> VM.flags for effective flags, -Xlog:gc*,gc+ergo*=debug to see G1's sizing decisions, -Xlog:gc+init for GC threads, and compare GC CPU% from JFR.
  5. Root cause: Mixing hand-tuned generational sizing with G1's pause-driven adaptive sizing. -Xmn/SurvivorRatio fix young size, so G1 cannot trade young size for pause time and old is starved; a 5 ms goal pushes it to tiny young regions anyway.
  6. Fix: Short-term: -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100. Remove -Xmn, SurvivorRatio, UseConcMarkSweepGC, and ParallelGCThreads (let ergonomics use 8). Long-term: if p99 must be below ~20 ms, evaluate ZGC instead of lowering the G1 goal.
  7. Prevention: Keep a reviewed, version-pinned flag file; CI check java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal against an allowlist; GC logs always on.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep -Xmn "for predictability" (it removes G1's main advantage), and I would not set the pause goal under ~50-100 ms; G1 can't honor it and throughput suffers. DisableExplicitGC is a judgment call: it breaks direct-buffer cleanup via System.gc() (use -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent instead).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does G1 reduce young size for a tighter goal? → Young pause cost scales with survivors/copy volume; fewer regions means smaller predicted pause.
  • What if the heap must be 4g but container is 4.5g? → Native memory (metaspace, threads, code cache) overshoots; leave headroom, see J1.
  • Is -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 default also fine? → Yes, default 200 ms; tune from measurements.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An old shared "JVM flags" wiki page was copied into 40 services. After one JDK upgrade several failed to start, others ran with stale CMS-era sizing. We replaced it with a minimal default (G1 or ZGC, container-aware MaxRAMPercentage) and justified every override in review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the pause value only, no mention of Xmn or invalid flags.
  • Hire: identifies Xmn conflict, unrealistic goal, and CMS removal.
  • Strong hire: also explains G1's adaptive model, uses VM.flags/gc+ergo to verify, and proposes a flag governance process.

questions.promptHtml: When would you pick Parallel GC over G1 and what exactly are you trading? What does MaxGCPauseMillis actually do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand throughput vs latency vs footprint, not just "G1 is default".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Parallel does multi-threaded stop-the-world young and full collections with the simplest barriers and no concurrent work, so it gets the best raw throughput and lowest overhead, but pauses scale with heap and live data. G1 pays barrier cost, remembered-set memory and concurrent threads to bound pauses. I pick Parallel for batch/offline jobs where total time matters, G1 when requests wait on pauses. MaxGCPauseMillis is a soft goal that G1 uses to size young and pick the collection set, not a limit."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect Parallel G1
Barriers Simple card-mark post-write Card mark plus SATB pre-write barrier plus refinement
Remembered sets One card table Per-region sets, extra memory
Concurrent work None Marking, refinement threads
Old collection Full STW (compacting) Mostly incremental mixed GCs
Pause scaling With old live set on Full GC Bounded by goal, mostly
Throughput Often a few percent better Slightly lower

Typical guidance: throughput difference is workload dependent, commonly single digit percent; measure rather than quote.

MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200): G1 predicts pause cost per region from past GCs and chooses young size and collection set to fit. Lower values mean smaller young, more frequent pauses, fewer old regions per mixed GC, more GC CPU and risk of losing the marking race. Docs warn very low values reduce throughput.

Parallel's equivalent: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis also exists and -XX:GCTimeRatio (default 99 => about 1% GC time target) drives its adaptive sizing (UseAdaptiveSizePolicy); verify both defaults.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Batch ETL on a 16-core box, JDK 21: total runtime matters
java -XX:+UseParallelGC -Xms24g -Xmx24g -jar etl.jar

# Request-serving API
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 -Xms8g -Xmx8g -jar api.jar

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming G1 is always better; for a 10-minute batch job on a dedicated box, Parallel often finishes sooner.
  • Treating the pause goal as an SLA.
  • Using Parallel for a service with a 30 GB live set: Full GC pauses in the tens of seconds.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Parallel faster? → No SATB, no concurrent threads, cheaper barriers, full CPU for the app between pauses.
  2. When is G1 slower than Parallel by a lot? → Heavy reference-write workloads (barrier cost), tiny CPU quotas (concurrent threads compete).
  3. How do you measure the choice? → Same load test, compare throughput, GC CPU%, and p99 under both.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Parallel for throughput." Senior explains barrier and remembered-set costs, treats the goal as a model input, and decides from measurements.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A nightly job moved to G1 by default and ran 12% longer; going back to Parallel saved a node-hour per night (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: How do you size the heap and the young generation for a service? Why do people set -Xms equal to -Xmx, and what does that cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Sizing is the most common tuning job; the bad answers are cargo cult.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I start from the measured live set after full-cycle GC, then give roughly 2-3x that as heap so the collector has room, and make Xms equal Xmx to avoid resize pauses and surprises. In G1/ZGC I leave young sizing to the collector. The cost is committed memory from the start, which matters in containers, so I also leave non-heap headroom."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Method:

  1. Run realistic load, take the live set = heap after old-gen collection (post-mixed/Full or ZGC cycle).
  2. Heap target ~ 2-3x live set (rule of thumb; lower for ZGC non-generational needs headroom for concurrent allocation, verify by load test).
  3. Check allocation rate (MB/s) from logs: young GC frequency = Eden size / alloc rate. 200 MB/s with 2 GB Eden => a young GC every ~10 s.
  4. Cap pause with the collector (G1 goal), not by shrinking Eden manually.

Equal Xms/Xmx: no grow/shrink cycles, memory committed up front (pages may be touched lazily; -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch forces it, slow start but no page-fault stalls).

Container: use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (default 25%; set e.g. 60-75) rather than hard-coded Xmx if pods vary; off-heap (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache) needs its own budget (see J1).

Generational sizing knobs (Serial/Parallel): -XX:NewRatio (old:young, default 2), -XX:SurvivorRatio (default 8: Eden:each survivor), -Xmn. For G1, G1NewSizePercent/G1MaxNewSizePercent exist but the default behavior is usually correct.

Heap 8g, Parallel NewRatio=2: Young ~2.67g -> Eden ~2.13g, S0=S1~0.27g
Alloc 300 MB/s -> Eden fills every ~7 s

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-Xms6g -Xmx6g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch              # fixed, pre-faulted heap
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=70   # container-relative

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sizing heap to nearly the container limit: OOMKilled by native memory.
  • Making young huge to cut GC count; each young GC can then promote more and copy more.
  • Tuning without live-set data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not a very large heap? → Longer Full GC / marking, bigger remembered sets, more RAM cost, hides leaks.
  2. Does a bigger heap always lower GC cost? → Frequency drops (Eden bigger) but the live-set copy cost per cycle stays; for G1, mixed cost scales with old regions picked.
  3. What does AlwaysPreTouch trade? → Slower startup, avoids runtime page faults and gives predictable latency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Xms=Xmx." Senior derives sizing from live set and allocation rate, shows the math, and accounts for non-heap and cgroup limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service at -Xmx7g in an 8 GB pod got OOMKilled weekly from metaspace plus Netty direct buffers; dropping heap to 5 GB ended it (illustrative).

questions.contextHtml:
Order service on Java 17, G1, 6 GB heap, 2000 RPS. After a feature launch that caches order history for 24 h, alerts fire: p99 jumped from 90 ms to 2.5 s every ~20 minutes. Logs:

[6221.4s][info][gc] GC(512) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 5400M->5200M(6144M) 310.4ms
[6221.7s][info][gc,heap] To-space exhausted
[6224.9s][info][gc] GC(513) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 5900M->4800M(6144M) 2480ms

Heap after Full GC stays at ~4.8 GB. Prior to launch, post-GC heap was ~1.9 GB.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more heap" or "switch to ZGC" without establishing that live set tripled. Possibly also "tune IHOP" without noticing the live set is the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed (the new cache)? Its size bound/TTL/eviction? Heap before vs after launch? Traffic growth? Any container memory limit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag the cache off or shrink TTL/size; as a stopgap raise heap to 10 GB if pod limit allows and restart one canary to confirm.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) live set grew from 1.9 GB to ~4.8 GB, leaving no evacuation headroom. (b) Reserve too small for the promotion rate. (c) Humongous allocations in cache values. (d) Leak in cache. Red herring: the 310 ms mixed pause itself; it is a symptom of evacuating nearly-full old.
  4. How I'd verify each: GC log trend of post-GC heap; jcmd GC.heap_info; heap histogram jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram; JFR jdk.OldObjectSample for leak candidates; check gc+humongous.
  5. Root cause: To-space exhausted means G1 could not find free regions to copy survivors into mid-evacuation. With 5.4 GB used of 6.1 GB, mixed GCs had no free regions as targets; G1 handled the failure by pinning objects in place, then fell back to a 2.5 s Full GC. Live set (4.8 GB of 6.1 GB, 78%) is far above the 2-3x guideline.
  6. Fix: Short-term: bounded cache (e.g. Caffeine maximumSize/expireAfterWrite), heap to 12 GB (live 4.8 GB * 2.5). Long-term: move history to Redis or a DB-backed read path.
  7. Prevention: Alert on post-GC heap > 60% of max, Full GC count > 0, evacuation-failure logs; load-test caches with production-sized data.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't lower IHOP or raise G1ReservePercent as the main fix; they delay the symptom but a 78% live set is a sizing/design problem.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would ZGC fix it? → It avoids long pauses but needs headroom too; at 78% occupancy you get allocation stalls instead.
  • Why is the Full GC single-digit seconds not worse? → Parallel full compaction since JDK 10; with more cores it scales.
  • How do you tell leak from legitimate growth? → Does post-GC heap plateau after TTL elapses (24 h)? A plateau means sizing, a ramp means leak.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" cache with TTL but no size bound plateaued only after 24 hours, so staging never exposed it. Production's Full GCs began exactly one day after deploy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases heap blindly or restarts.
  • Hire: identifies live set growth and to-space exhaustion, proposes bounding the cache.
  • Strong hire: explains evacuation mechanics, uses post-GC trend, plateau-vs-ramp test, and sets alerts.

questions.promptHtml: What is a write barrier and a card table? How do barriers differ between Parallel, G1, and ZGC?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Barriers explain the throughput cost of each collector and why collectors can't be swapped for free.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A barrier is a small piece of code the JIT inserts around reference reads or writes so the collector can track what the application changes. Parallel marks a card on reference writes so young GC knows which old regions to scan. G1 adds an SATB pre-write barrier for concurrent marking and a post-write barrier feeding remembered sets. ZGC uses load barriers, checking pointer metadata on every reference load so it can fix pointers lazily during concurrent relocation."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Parallel/Serial post-write:    obj.field = ref;  card_table[addr(obj) >> 9] = DIRTY
G1 pre-write (SATB):           if (marking_active) log(old value of obj.field)
G1 post-write:                 if cross-region: enqueue card for refinement into region's remembered set
ZGC load barrier:              ref = obj.field; if (bad color bits) slow_path(ref)  // heal pointer
  • Card table: heap split into 512-byte cards; one byte per card. Young GC scans only dirty old cards for old-to-young pointers.
  • G1 SATB pre-barrier: during concurrent mark, overwritten references are recorded so the marker sees the object graph as at the start (no lost live objects). Cost: a branch on every reference store, more work during marking.
  • G1 remembered sets: per region, populated by refinement threads from dirty cards; allows collecting arbitrary regions.
  • ZGC load barrier: the JIT emits a check of the loaded pointer's metadata bits; when the pointer is stale (object relocated, or in a stage needing marking), the slow path marks/remaps it. Later-generation ZGC adds store barriers for generational tracking (JEP 439 notes; verify detail).
  • Shenandoah uses a load-reference barrier (see Q035).

Consequences: barriers affect throughput (ZGC/Shenandoah typically a few percent to ~15% depending on workload; measure), cause the application to do GC work (healing), and the cost is per reference access/store, so pointer-heavy code pays more.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// What the JIT sees conceptually
Node n = head.next;     // ZGC: load barrier on this reference read
head.next = other;      // G1/Parallel: write barrier (card mark; G1 also SATB when marking)
int x = n.value;        // primitive read: no barrier

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "ZGC has no overhead". It trades pause for barrier/throughput overhead.
  • Saying barriers exist only during GC. Most check cheaply always; slow paths fire only during phases.
  • Confusing card tables (cheap, one structure) with G1 remembered sets (per region, memory-heavy).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why SATB instead of incremental update? → Simplifies termination of concurrent marking, no need to rescan roots; cost is floating garbage.
  2. What is floating garbage? → Objects that die after marking started but are still treated as live until the next cycle.
  3. Why do arrays of primitives not have barriers? → No references to track.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "barriers track writes." Senior distinguishes store vs load barriers per collector and links them to throughput and latency characteristics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reference-heavy graph service lost ~8% throughput moving from Parallel to ZGC; capacity planning had assumed zero overhead (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: How does ZGC achieve sub-millisecond-class pauses regardless of heap size? What stays stop-the-world and what is the cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers must reason about why concurrent collectors have different failure modes (allocation stalls) from G1.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "ZGC does marking, relocation and reference processing concurrently. Its STW pauses are only brief root-scanning and phase-transition handshakes, whose duration doesn't scale with heap or live set. It relies on load barriers and pointer metadata so threads can see and heal relocated objects while the app runs. The price is barrier overhead, CPU spent by concurrent GC threads, no compressed oops, and the need for headroom or you get allocation stalls."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cycle (JDK 21 non-generational flavor; verify details per release):

  1. Pause Mark Start (STW, tiny): scan thread roots.
  2. Concurrent Mark/Remap: traverse heap; objects marked via pointer color bits in the reference.
  3. Pause Mark End (STW, tiny), then concurrent reference processing and selecting relocation set.
  4. Pause Relocate Start (STW, tiny).
  5. Concurrent Relocate: copy live objects out of sparse pages; a forwarding table maps old to new addresses. Any thread (GC or mutator via load barrier) that touches an old pointer relocates or remaps it ("self-healing").

Key design points:

  • Colored pointers / metadata bits in 64-bit references encode GC state; this means no compressed oops and a max heap of 16 TB (verify per version).
  • Pages: small (2 MB), medium (32 MB), large (>= 4 MB objects, one per page; verify sizes).
  • Pause time is independent of heap size because STW work is root scanning only (thread count matters: very many threads lengthen it).
  • Allocation stall: if the app allocates faster than ZGC can free, threads block until memory frees. Shows up in logs as Allocation Stall.
  • Tuning is minimal: -Xmx (leave headroom), -XX:SoftMaxHeapSize (soft target; JDK 13+), -XX:ConcGCThreads, -XX:ZUncommit. -XX:ZCollectionInterval forces periodic cycles.
 app threads -----------------------------------------------> (load barrier heals)
 GC:  |pause|====concurrent mark====|pause|==relocate (concurrent)==|
       <1ms                           <1ms

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx16g -XX:SoftMaxHeapSize=12g -Xlog:gc* -jar app.jar   # JDK 21
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xmx16g -jar app.jar                                                          # JDK 23+: generational by default

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating low pause with low latency; throughput loss and stalls still hurt p99.
  • Running ZGC at 90% heap occupancy: stalls.
  • Ignoring that heap RSS may exceed Xmx accounting due to multi-mapped memory showing in tools (pmap oddities); measure with NMT/cgroup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why no compressed oops? → Pointer metadata bits take the high bits of the reference; heap addresses are full 64-bit.
  2. What happens when GC can't keep up? → Allocation stalls; fix with more headroom, more concurrent threads, or reduce allocation rate.
  3. What does a very high thread count do? → Longer root scanning pauses and handshakes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ZGC is low pause." Senior explains load barriers, self-healing, pause independence from heap size, and the allocation-stall failure mode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A matching engine met 5 ms p99 on ZGC only after raising headroom from 15% to 40% of the heap; before that stalls added 30-100 ms (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: What did Generational ZGC change, and which Java version do you use which flag on? Should I just enable it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Version-specific knowledge: a common source of wrong configs on JDK 21.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Non-generational ZGC collected the whole heap every cycle, so it burned CPU re-marking long-lived data and needed lots of headroom. Generational ZGC (JEP 439, JDK 21, opt-in with -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational) adds young and old generations so most work targets young objects. In JDK 23 it became the default under -XX:+UseZGC (JEP 474) and JDK 24 removed the non-generational mode (JEP 490)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timeline verified from OpenJDK JEP pages:

JDK -XX:+UseZGC means
15-20 non-generational ZGC (production since 15)
21 non-generational; add -XX:+ZGenerational for generational
23 generational by default; -XX:-ZGenerational selects old mode (deprecated)
24+ non-generational removed (JEP 490, targeted JDK 24; verify in release notes)

Why it matters (JEP 439 goals): lower allocation-stall risk, lower heap overhead, lower GC CPU overhead, with pauses staying sub-millisecond-class and no manual tuning of generation sizes or tenuring.

Mechanism differences: the young collection runs more often and cheaper; survivor objects move to old; ZGC adds store barriers and a remembered set so young collections need not scan the old gen; the load barrier remains. Memory-copy of young survivors is concurrent.

Should you enable it? On 21: for alloc-heavy services that struggled with non-generational ZGC (stalls, high CPU), usually yes, but run your own load test; for steady low-alloc workloads the gain is smaller. Don't rely on benchmark claims without testing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# JDK 21 LTS
java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx12g -jar app.jar
# JDK 25 LTS
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xmx12g -jar app.jar

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting only -XX:+UseZGC on 21 and thinking you have generational ZGC.
  • Keeping -XX:+ZGenerational on 24+ (option obsolete: warnings; verify).
  • Comparing heap numbers across modes without re-sizing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does generational help ZGC's allocation stalls? → Young garbage is reclaimed more frequently without re-marking the whole heap.
  2. What new barrier cost appears? → Store barriers to maintain the remembered set.
  3. Does it change the pause profile? → No; goal is still sub-millisecond-class.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "generational ZGC exists." Senior gives per-version flag behavior, the reasons, and demands measurement before migrating.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team upgrading 17 to 21 enabled UseZGC alone, saw the old behavior, and spent days tuning heap before noticing the missing flag (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: How does Shenandoah get low pauses, and how does it differ from ZGC? Where is it available?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests breadth and honest knowledge of vendor availability and modes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Shenandoah is a region-based collector that evacuates concurrently, so pauses don't scale with heap. It uses a load-reference barrier to find the current copy of an object during concurrent copying. It is not in Oracle builds but ships in Red Hat, Corretto, Zulu and others. Default mode is single-generation SATB; a generational mode became a product feature in JDK 25."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Heap is regions like G1. Cycle: init mark (STW), concurrent mark (SATB), final mark (STW), concurrent cleanup/evacuation, init/final update refs (STW, short), concurrent update refs. Pause durations are small and independent of heap size.
  • Forwarding: originally via a Brooks pointer (an extra word per object) and now via a load-reference barrier in newer versions (verify exact JDK where the switch occurred; the wiki mentions "forwarding pointer with each object" in its barrier description).
  • Pointers are not colored, so compressed oops stay usable, a footprint advantage over ZGC (ZGC needs full 64-bit).
  • Availability per wiki: mainline in 11u (since 11.0.9), 17, 21, 25 but vendor-dependent; Oracle does not ship it.
  • Modes via -XX:ShenandoahGCMode: satb (default), generational (JDK 25 product, JEP 521; experimental in 24), passive (diagnostic). Heuristics (adaptive default for non-generational; verify): -XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=adaptive|compact|static|aggressive.
  • Trade-offs vs ZGC: Shenandoah works with compressed oops and smaller heaps, adapts by heuristic, but is vendor-dependent; ZGC ships with Oracle OpenJDK, scales to multi-TB heaps and has had more investment in generational mode earlier (JDK 21).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -Xmx8g -jar app.jar                       # JDK 21 on a vendor with Shenandoah
java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational -Xmx8g -jar app.jar   # JDK 25 (verify)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming -XX:+UseShenandoahGC works on any JDK; HotSpot builds without it say "unrecognized".
  • Believing Shenandoah has no allocation-failure mode: it has "pacing" and degenerated/full GC fallbacks.
  • Mixing up GC modes (ShenandoahGCHeuristics warns in generational mode).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is pacing? → Throttling allocating threads when GC lags (analogous to ZGC stalls but gentler); verify exact semantics.
  2. Degenerated GC? → Fallback to STW collection when concurrent cycle can't finish in time.
  3. Why choose Shenandoah on a 4 GB heap? → Compressed oops keep footprint low while delivering low pauses.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "another low-pause GC." Senior contrasts barrier design, compressed oops, availability, and fallback behavior.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team on an Oracle JDK image could not use Shenandoah; moving to a Corretto base image was required, and nobody had checked the vendor table until the flag failed at startup.

questions.contextHtml: You own three JVM workloads on Java 21 in Kubernetes (all on 4-8 vCPU nodes): (A) Public REST API, 4 GB heap, 1500 RPS, SLO p99 < 200 ms, allocation ~250 MB/s, live set 1 GB. (B) Nightly Spark-like batch in plain Java, 24 GB heap, runs 3 hours, SLO is finishing before 6 am. (C) Real-time bidding service, 16 GB heap, p99 < 15 ms, allocation 1.5 GB/s, live set 5 GB. Each team asks "which GC?"
questions.promptHtml: Recommend a collector and key flags for each, with reasoning and the measurements you want before committing.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ZGC for all, it's the best" or "G1 for all, it's the default," without reasoning on pause, throughput, footprint.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Current GC logs and p99 breakdown (is GC even the cause)? CPU headroom and cost constraints? Heap growth patterns? Can I load-test with production traces?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). Baseline each with GC logging on and a replay load test.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • A: G1 default is enough; 200 ms SLO vs G1 typical tens of ms pauses at 4 GB. Cheapest, well-trodden.
    • B: Parallel; throughput is the metric and pauses are irrelevant.
    • C: ZGC (generational with -XX:+ZGenerational on 21) or Shenandoah if on a vendor build, because 15 ms p99 with 1.5 GB/s allocation exceeds what G1 can reliably bound.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the same load test per candidate; compare p99/p999, GC CPU%, throughput, RSS. For C, watch Allocation Stall logs and concurrent GC CPU.
  5. Root cause (of the choice): Match the collector to the constraint: latency tail (C), throughput (B), simplicity/footprint (A).
  6. Fix (flags): A: -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100. B: -XX:+UseParallelGC -Xms24g -Xmx24g. C: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xms16g -Xmx16g with headroom: live 5 GB gives about 3x ratio, and a CPU quota that leaves room for GC threads.
  7. Prevention: Record the decision and the benchmark, alert on GC CPU and pause p99, re-evaluate on JDK upgrade.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not ZGC for B (barrier overhead, no benefit). Not squeezing C below ~2 CPUs per instance; GC and app compete. Not tuning A beyond the pause goal unless measured.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• C's budget forces 4 GB heap? → Allocation stalls rise; reduce allocation (object pooling, primitives) or accept more nodes.
  • A moves to 2 vCPU pods? → Check for Serial fallback and concurrent thread contention.
  • What if C must run on Oracle JDK 17? → Non-generational ZGC (production since 15) or G1 with measured tuning.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company standardized on one GC across all services. The standard was fine for APIs but made the nightly jobs 15% slower and cost real money in node-hours; we split the standard into profiles.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one collector for everything without reasoning.
  • Hire: correct mapping with pause/throughput reasoning.
  • Strong hire: includes measurement plan, headroom/CPU costs, version-specific flags, and the cost of being wrong.

questions.contextHtml:
Pricing service, Java 21, -XX:+UseZGC (not generational), 10 GB heap in a 12 GB pod, 6 vCPU. Black Friday traffic doubles to 4000 RPS. p99 jumps from 25 ms to 400 ms though GC pauses in logs are all < 1 ms. Excerpt:

[3402.1s][info][gc] GC(881) Garbage Collection (Allocation Rate) 9100M(89%)->8900M(87%)
[3402.4s][info][gc] Allocation Stall (http-nio-8080-exec-17) 87.3ms
[3402.4s][info][gc] Allocation Stall (http-nio-8080-exec-3) 91.0ms

CPU is 95%, live set ~6.5 GB. A colleague says "ZGC pauses are sub-ms, so GC is not the problem."
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Trusts the pause number, hunts the DB; or randomly adds heap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Allocation rate now vs before? Was there a deploy? CPU quota (GC threads share it)? Heap max vs pod limit headroom?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scale pods out (reduce per-pod allocation rate), and if memory allows raise heap to 14 GB on canaries.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) allocation rate outpaces concurrent GC, causing allocation stalls (logs say so). (b) CPU saturation starves GC threads (95% CPU). (c) live set 65% of heap leaves only 35% headroom. (d) Red herring: DB latency, as GC logs show stalls directly.
  4. How I'd verify each: grep "Allocation Stall" count/duration; -Xlog:gc+init/jcmd GC.heap_info; async-profiler alloc mode to rank allocation sites; JFR jdk.GCPhaseConcurrent and jdk.ZAllocationStall (verify event name); CPU per thread (top -H) to see ZWorker threads.
  5. Root cause: Non-generational ZGC must trace the whole 6.5 GB live set each cycle. At doubled allocation rate the app consumed the remaining 3.5 GB faster than a cycle could free memory, and with CPU at 95% the concurrent workers could not catch up. Stall threads block until memory is freed; that is request latency invisible to "pause" metrics.
  6. Fix: Short-term: more heap (10 -> 14 GB, headroom to ~55%), more pods, -XX:ConcGCThreads modestly up if CPU allows. Medium-term: switch to -XX:+ZGenerational (JDK 21), which cuts re-marking of long-lived data. Long-term: cut allocation (profile top sites, e.g. per-request JSON trees) and dedupe cached objects.
  7. Prevention: Alert on Allocation Stall count and p99 per GC mode; capacity-test at 2x peak; track allocation rate (MB/s) as a first-class metric.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add pods blindly if the CPU was already saturated by GC; I would not switch to G1 as a reflex (we would trade stalls for longer pauses at 4000 RPS).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would SoftMaxHeapSize help? → It makes ZGC collect earlier, trading CPU for headroom; useful if memory can't grow.
  • Why don't stalls show as pauses? → Only the allocating thread blocks; no safepoint.
  • Container memory 12 GB, heap 14 GB? → Not possible; raise the pod limit too.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Dashboards plotted only GC pause p99, which read 0.4 ms all day. After we added a stall counter the graph correlated perfectly with latency alarms; the team had trusted the wrong signal for months.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames network/DB, ignores the stall log.
  • Hire: identifies allocation stalls and adds headroom.
  • Strong hire: ties to live set and CPU, proposes generational ZGC, profiles allocation, adds the right metric.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the relationship between allocation rate, live set, heap size, GC frequency and GC pause. How would you reason about a change in each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The mental model behind every tuning decision, and where candidates show real depth with numbers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Frequency of young GC is allocation rate divided by Eden size. Pause duration is driven by live data surviving that cycle plus root and remembered-set work, not by garbage or total heap. For old collections, cost scales with the live set. So more heap lowers frequency, more live data raises per-collection cost and reduces headroom, and a higher allocation rate raises frequency and promotion pressure."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Worked example: heap 8 GB, G1, Eden ~4 GB at steady state, allocation 400 MB/s.

  • Young GC every 4096/400 ~= 10.2 s.
  • If 3% survives each cycle: 4096 * 0.03 = ~123 MB copied. At ~1 GB/s copy throughput per the pause machinery (illustrative), that is ~120 ms.
  • Double allocation to 800 MB/s: GC every ~5 s, same survivors each cycle if survival ratio holds, so pause is similar but GC CPU doubles in relative terms. But survivors per second double, so old promotion rate doubles: old fills twice as fast, and marking must start earlier.
  • Live set growth from 1 GB to 4 GB: young pauses unchanged, mixed pauses and marking time rise, headroom falls, Full GC risk up.

Rules:

young GC interval  = Eden size / allocation rate
young GC pause     ~ survivors (bytes) * copy cost + roots + dirty cards
GC CPU %           ~ (pause * frequency) + concurrent threads
promotion rate     ~ alloc rate * survival fraction past tenuring
old fill time      = free old / promotion rate  (must exceed mark + mixed time)

Levers: reduce allocation (fix code), reduce live set (cache bounds), increase heap (frequency, headroom), adjust collector.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Reduce allocation rate: avoid per-request garbage
String s = "";                        // broken: O(n) allocations in loops
for (var p : parts) s += p;
var sb = new StringBuilder(parts.size() * 16);   // one buffer
for (var p : parts) sb.append(p);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "More heap fixes pauses" (only true when frequency, not live set, is the problem).
  • Measuring allocation as heap growth; use GC log deltas (before-after) or JFR jdk.ThreadAllocationStatistics.
  • Ignoring that allocation inside request threads multiplies by RPS.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you measure allocation rate? → From GC logs: (used before this GC - used after previous GC)/time; or JFR allocation statistics; async-profiler alloc.
  2. Why can a smaller young reduce pauses but hurt throughput? → Fewer survivors per GC but more GCs and earlier promotion.
  3. What dominates a Full GC? → Live set size (mark + compact).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "more memory, fewer GCs." Senior computes intervals and promotion rates, knows what scales with what, and chooses the lever by cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service's p99 doubled at 2x traffic. Pause stayed constant but GC frequency doubled and CPU saturation turned it into queueing; fixing a per-request allocation hotspot gave a 35% rate reduction (illustrative).

questions.contextHtml:
Event-processing service, Java 11, G1, 30 GB heap (-Xms30g -Xmx30g), 16 vCPU. Each night p99 spikes. GC log excerpt:

[1520.1s][info][gc] GC(204) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 27800M->26900M(30720M) 140ms
[1520.2s][info][gc] GC(205) Concurrent Cycle
[1535.9s][info][gc] GC(206) Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 30200M->25100M(30720M) 31400ms
[1567.5s][info][gc] GC(207) Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 30300M->25000M(30720M) 30900ms

Live set after Full GC is ~25 GB; steady-state used heap before the nightly job was ~9 GB. The job loads a 16 GB reference dataset.
questions.promptHtml: Why are Full GCs repeating, and what do you do now and next?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap or lower MaxGCPauseMillis." Doesn't notice the live set (25 GB of 30) leaves nothing for any collector.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the 16 GB dataset be partitioned or memory-mapped? How is it held (objects, arrays, maps)? Is the box memory-bound? Does the job need to run alongside live traffic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the nightly job or run it on a dedicated instance; if needed restart with the job off-peak; do not leave a service in a Full GC loop.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) live set 83% of heap: no free space to copy/evacuate; concurrent cycle started at 27.8 GB used, way too late (IHOP triggered too late because live data jumped). (b) fragmentation/humongous objects from big arrays. (c) Java 11 G1 Full GC being single-threaded! Fact: G1 Full GC became parallel in JDK 10 (JEP 307), so on 11 it's parallel; 31 s still because 25 GB must be marked and compacted. Red herring: GC thread count.
  4. How I'd verify each: -Xlog:gc*,gc+humongous=debug, heap histogram, jcmd GC.class_histogram, and MAT on a heap dump to see what holds 16 GB.
  5. Root cause: The workload's live set (25 GB) approaches max heap (30 GB). Each evacuation or allocation failure forces a compacting Full GC that frees only ~5 GB, which is immediately consumed. Pause grows linearly with live data; 31 s ~= 25 GB / ~0.8 GB/s (illustrative).
  6. Fix: Short-term: heap to ~60 GB (about 2.4x live) if node memory permits, or run the job separately with smaller footprint. Long-term: store the dataset off-heap (memory-mapped file, columnar long[]/ByteBuffer), or stream-process it; consider ZGC or Shenandoah if large live data is permanent and the pauses matter (still needs headroom).
  7. Prevention: Alert on post-GC occupancy > 60-70%; test the nightly job against production-size data; add a heap budget in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not tune IHOP/pause goal as the fix; not adopt ZGC while live set is 83% of heap; ZGC would just stall.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the node only has 32 GB RAM? → Must reduce live set or go off-heap; collectors can't create memory.
  • Would -XX:+UseStringDeduplication help? → Only if the dataset has many duplicate Strings; needs measuring.
  • Why concurrent cycle started so late? → Adaptive IHOP predicted from a low prior allocation rate; the job's load changed behavior abruptly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" nightly aggregation loaded all rows into HashMap<String, List<Row>> in the serving JVM. Rewriting it to external sort + streaming removed the incident class entirely.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts and raises Xmx without analysis.
  • Hire: identifies live-set/headroom problem and separates the job.
  • Strong hire: quantifies headroom, explains why GC tuning cannot help, proposes off-heap/streaming and alerts.

questions.contextHtml: Checkout service (Java 21, G1, 12 GB heap, 24 pods, 3000 RPS total) has p99 = 180 ms and p999 = 900 ms, with G1 pauses of 80-250 ms on bursts. Product wants p999 < 150 ms before a sale in 6 weeks. You propose Generational ZGC. Risk owner asks how you would roll it out without breaking checkout.
questions.promptHtml: Describe the migration plan and what could go wrong.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Change the flag and deploy to all pods."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is GC actually the p999 contributor (compare against GC pause log timestamps)? CPU headroom per pod? Heap live set? Does any dependency rely on compressed oops-specific sizing or on -XX:+UseG1GC-specific flags?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is a planned change. Keep rollback to G1 as one config flip.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Gains: (a) pauses vanish; (b) p999 improvement if GC was the cause. Risks: (c) barrier overhead of a few percent throughput; (d) memory growth because no compressed oops (G1 with a 12 GB heap uses compressed oops; ZGC does not, so object footprint rises, often 10-30%, verify with your data); (e) allocation stalls if headroom thin; (f) monitoring tools/flags differ.
  4. How I'd verify each: Offline: replay production traffic (k6 or recorded traces) at 1.5x peak against both configs; compare p99/p999, CPU, RSS, Allocation Stall. Canary: 1 pod then 10%, compare against G1 pods in the same traffic via metrics.
  5. Root cause (of choice): Confirm G1 pauses align with p999 spikes via timestamps before concluding.
  6. Fix (plan): Flags -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xms12g -Xmx16g (extra headroom for no compressed oops; verify with the test); remove G1-specific flags; same JDK build; ramp 1 -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over days with automatic rollback on p999 regression or stall count. Keep a few G1 pods during the sale as control.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards for stalls, GC CPU, RSS, and per-GC-mode latency; runbook for rollback; note in service docs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not combine with other upgrades (JDK or framework) in the same rollout; not rely on synthetic microbenchmarks; not remove G1 option until after the sale.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Canary p999 is better but CPU is up 12%? → Capacity plan (more pods) or accept; cost vs latency decision, quantify.
  • Memory-limited pods? → Raise limits or skip migration; ZGC needs headroom.
  • Result mixed across traffic types? → Segment by endpoint; check if tails are GC or downstream.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: We found p999 spikes did not match GC timestamps at all; they came from a DB failover pattern. The migration was cancelled, saving weeks, because we validated the premise first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips flag everywhere.
  • Hire: canary, rollback, load test.
  • Strong hire: validates premise, accounts for compressed-oops/footprint, control group, and sale-period freeze.

questions.promptHtml: "ZGC and Shenandoah are pauseless." True? What pauses remain, what else can stop your threads, and what affects their duration?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates marketing from mechanism; leads to safepoints and time-to-safepoint discussion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Not pauseless. They have very short STW phases for root scanning and phase handoffs, plus JVM-wide safepoint operations for other reasons (deoptimization, class redefinition, biased-lock-era revocations, thread dumps). Pause duration depends on thread count, root set size, and time-to-safepoint, not heap size. And non-pause stalls (allocation stalls, pacing, barrier slow paths) can hurt latency without appearing as pauses."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Safepoint: a point where all Java threads are stopped at known states so the VM can run an operation. A collector's STW phase needs one. Time-to-safepoint (TTSP) is the time for all threads to reach it; a long counted loop without a safepoint poll historically delayed it (improved by loop strip mining in newer JDKs).
  • Remaining STW phases: ZGC has mark start, mark end, relocate start; Shenandoah has init mark, final mark, init update refs, final update refs. Each scales with GC roots (thread stacks, JNI handles, class loader data) and not with heap size.
  • Other safepoint ops: deoptimization, class redefinition (agents), Thread.print/heap dump (jmap -dump forces a safepoint), code cache sweeps, "ICBufferFull", biased-lock revocation (biased locking disabled by default in JDK 15, removed later; verify).
  • Non-pause tail latency: allocation stalls (ZGC), pacing and degenerated GCs (Shenandoah), barrier slow paths, GC thread CPU contention, page-fault stalls (without pretouch), System.gc().

Diagnose: -Xlog:safepoint* shows reason, TTSP and operation time per safepoint.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-Xlog:safepoint*:file=sp.log:time,uptime
# Look at: "Safepoint "ZMarkStart", Time since last: ..., Reaching safepoint: 1200000 ns, At safepoint: 300000 ns"
// A long counted loop can delay safepoint arrival on some JDKs/JITs
for (int i = 0; i < Integer.MAX_VALUE; i++) { sum += arr[i & mask]; }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading only GC pause metrics; safepoint logs contain the non-GC stops.
  • Blaming GC for pauses caused by jmap -dump taken during an incident.
  • Assuming 5,000 threads is free for root scanning.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is TTSP? → The delay until all threads reach the safepoint; the VM waits for the slowest.
  2. What does -XX:+PrintSafepointStatistics map to now? → Replaced by unified -Xlog:safepoint.
  3. Does System.gc() stop the world in ZGC? → It triggers a full concurrent cycle; the app waits only as a caller; -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent/DisableExplicitGC options exist.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ZGC has sub-ms pauses." Senior distinguishes GC phases from other safepoint ops and non-pause latency, and uses safepoint logs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "pauseless" GC service still stalled 300 ms periodically; a monitoring agent was triggering heap histograms with -all, forcing safepoints (illustrative).

questions.contextHtml: After moving a Java 17 service from VMs (8 vCPU, 16 GB) to Kubernetes with resources.limits: cpu: "1", memory: "2Gi", latency worsened. Pre-migration G1 pauses were ~40 ms; now the first deploy shows p99 up from 110 ms to 700 ms and GC pauses of 300-600 ms every few seconds. No flags were set except -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75. Heap is therefore ~1.5 GB. The post-incident review asks why, and what the standard should be.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: root cause, contributing factors, and the guardrails you would add.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Containers are slower; give it more CPU." No mention of collector selection or ergonomics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What collector is actually running? availableProcessors() seen by the JVM? Live set size? What else shares the 2 GiB (metaspace, threads, direct buffers)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise CPU limit to 2-4 and memory to fit; roll back to previous placement if SLO burn is active.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) with 1 CPU the JVM is not "server-class" (needs at least 2 CPUs and about 2 GB, verify exact rule), so it selects Serial GC, single-threaded stop-the-world. (b) CPU throttling (CFS quota) stalls GC threads. (c) 1.5 GB heap + native overhead near the 2 GiB limit. Red herring: network, since GC log correlates.
  4. How I'd verify each: java -Xlog:gc+init -version inside the container; jcmd <pid> VM.info; Runtime.availableProcessors(); cgroup cpu.stat for nr_throttled; NMT summary for non-heap.
  5. Root cause: Container CPU limit of 1 made ergonomics choose Serial GC and one GC thread; each young/full collection ran single-threaded and, under CFS throttling, was further paused by the kernel, making pauses look 10x longer.
  6. Fix: Short-term: CPU limit 2+ (or request 1/limit 2) and explicitly -XX:+UseG1GC; keep MaxRAMPercentage at 60-70 to leave native headroom. Long-term: platform default JVM profile (explicit collector, ActiveProcessorCount only if justified, GC logs on).
  7. Prevention: Startup log assertion of collector/CPU count; throttling alert on container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total; template with explicit collector flag; load test in the target resource shape before migration.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not force G1 on 1 CPU without testing (concurrent threads compete with the app); Serial may actually be right for tiny pods. Not remove CPU limits globally.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just set -XX:ParallelGCThreads=8? → Threads still share a 1-CPU quota; throttling worsens.
  • Should small pods use Serial on purpose? → For heaps under a few hundred MB and 1 CPU, often yes: lowest overhead.
  • What is -XX:ActiveProcessorCount? → Overrides CPU count seen by the JVM; use with care, it does not give you real CPU.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Dozens of services were "right-sized" to 1 CPU by an automated tool; half silently switched to Serial. A single startup log line, scraped into a dashboard, found them in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: asks for more CPU without diagnosing.
  • Hire: finds Serial fallback and throttling.
  • Strong hire: explains ergonomics rule, adds startup assertions, throttling alerts, and nuanced Serial-for-small-pods stance.

questions.contextHtml:
Search-indexing service on Java 21, G1, -Xmx6g, 200 MB/s allocation, young pauses 35 ms, mixed pauses 90 ms. Business plans 10x data: the in-memory index grows from 2 GB to 20 GB live, allocation rate to ~800 MB/s, on a 16 vCPU / 64 GB host. Product asks you to just set -Xmx48g and keep p99 under 200 ms. Early test with -Xmx48g, default flags, shows:

Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 31000M->24000M(49152M) 410ms
Pause Remark 22.4s...

(remark/cleanup times 150-300 ms; concurrent mark cycles take ~40 s).
questions.promptHtml: Will Xmx48g meet the p99 target? What do you evaluate and recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "G1 scales; set pause goal to 100 ms." Ignores that live data drives mixed-GC and marking cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the index mutate or is it read-mostly? Is the p99 target at request level or GC level? Latency of queries vs rebuild? Can the index be partitioned across pods or placed off-heap?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; capacity planning. Keep the test results as baseline.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) with 20 GB live, mixed GCs evacuate big old regions and remembered sets grow, so 410 ms exceeds the goal; (b) long marking (40 s) raises the risk of losing the race at 800 MB/s (each 40 s of promotion could consume many GB); (c) remembered set memory and refinement overhead grow with a pointer-heavy index; (d) red herring: compressed oops since 48 GB heap exceeds the ~32 GB threshold, making all pointers 8 bytes and growing the footprint (verify -Xlog:gc+init shows compressed oops disabled above ~32 GB).
  4. How I'd verify each: -Xlog:gc*,gc+phases=debug,gc+ergo*=debug; jcmd GC.class_histogram; check for to-space exhausted; compare object footprint at 28 GB vs 48 GB heap; JFR for refinement and card scanning.
  5. Root cause: Pause-bound collectors still do work proportional to live data touched per mixed GC; at 20 GB live the per-mixed cost is dominated by remembered sets and copy volume, and crossing the compressed-oops limit inflates the index.
  6. Fix: Evaluate three options by load test: (1) generational ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational on 21) at ~48-56 GB with 2.5x headroom; (2) keep G1 at ~28 GB heap (compressed oops) by moving most of the index off-heap or into memory-mapped/columnar long[] structures; (3) shard the index across pods (e.g. 4 x 8 GB heaps). My bet: sharding plus G1 for simplicity, ZGC as the alternative if sharding is infeasible.
  7. Prevention: Track live set, mixed GC duration, marking time, and compressed-oops status per release; enforce a heap budget in design reviews.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on MaxGCPauseMillis=100 to force pauses down; G1 will miss it and burn CPU. Not cross the ~32 GB heap line (exact limit depends on alignment; verify with -Xshare:dump or PrintFlagsFinal) without measuring footprint.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does 48 GB heap use more memory per object than 31 GB? → Compressed oops disabled: 8-byte references and bigger headers in some layouts.
  • Would a bigger young help? → It lowers frequency, not mixed cost from the live set.
  • Could Parallel work if the service tolerates pauses? → Full GC at 20 GB live would take many seconds; no.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team scaled heap up 8x for a cache and watched pause time grow almost linearly. They spent a quarter tuning flags, then solved it in a week by sharding and moving payloads to off-heap slabs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sets bigger heap and pause flag.
  • Hire: recognizes live set drives cost, evaluates ZGC and sharding.
  • Strong hire: includes compressed-oops threshold, marking-vs-promotion race math, load-test plan, and architecture alternatives.

questions.promptHtml: Give me the GC flags you would actually reach for on a modern JDK, their defaults, and which you'd refuse to set without evidence. How has this changed across Java 8, 11, 17, 21?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether your tuning is evidence-based and version-aware, not copy-pasted from old blog posts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I set the collector, the heap (Xms=Xmx or container percentage), GC logging, and maybe MaxGCPauseMillis for G1. I rarely touch everything else; G1 and ZGC are adaptive. I check defaults with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal per JDK, because they changed: default collector moved from Parallel to G1 in 9, CMS was removed in 14, ZGC went production in 15, and ZGC is generational by default from 23."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Flag Default / notes (verify with PrintFlagsFinal on your JDK)
-XX:+UseG1GC Default on server-class machines since JDK 9
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis 200 (G1 soft goal)
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent 45 (initial value; adaptive IHOP on)
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize ergonomic, 1-32 MB, power of two
-XX:G1NewSizePercent / G1MaxNewSizePercent 5 / 60 (percent of heap)
-XX:G1MixedGCCountTarget 8
-XX:G1ReservePercent 10
-XX:G1HeapWastePercent 5
-XX:ParallelGCThreads N if N<=8, else 8 + (N-8)*5/8
-XX:ConcGCThreads derived from ParallelGCThreads (about 1/4; verify)
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage 25 (hence the surprise of a 25% heap in containers)
-XX:+ZGenerational JDK 21 opt-in; default under UseZGC from 23; obsolete when the old mode was removed (24)
-XX:SoftMaxHeapSize ZGC (and Shenandoah in newer builds), soft limit
-Xlog:gc* Unified logging since JDK 9 (replaces PrintGCDetails)

Version changes: JDK 8 Parallel default, PermGen replaced by Metaspace; 9 G1 default and unified logging; 10 parallel full GC for G1 (JEP 307); 11 ZGC experimental, Epsilon added; 14 CMS removed; 15 ZGC and Shenandoah production; 21 generational ZGC; 23 generational ZGC default; 25 generational Shenandoah product.

Flags to be skeptical of: -Xmn/NewRatio/SurvivorRatio on G1 (kill adaptivity), -XX:+DisableExplicitGC (breaks direct-buffer cleanup patterns), very low MaxGCPauseMillis, G1ReservePercent and IHOP tweaks as a first response, -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch without understanding startup cost, -XX:ParallelGCThreads overrides in containers.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MaxGCPauseMillis|InitiatingHeapOccupancy|G1HeapRegionSize|MaxRAMPercentage|ParallelGCThreads"
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m -jar app.jar

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using flags from a Java 8 blog on 17 (PrintGCDetails is deprecated/removed form; CMS flags fail).
  • Believing defaults are universal; ergonomics depend on CPU/memory.
  • Tuning ten flags at once, so no attribution.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you know the running value of a flag? → jcmd <pid> VM.flags -all or jinfo -flag <name> <pid>.
  2. What is -XX:+UseStringDeduplication? → G1 (and others in newer JDKs) dedupes String backing arrays in the background; benefit workload-dependent.
  3. How would you tune after a flag change? → One change at a time, same load test, compare GC CPU, p99, throughput.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites flags. Senior states how little to set, how to verify, and which defaults moved across versions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service migrated with a 6-year-old flags file; UseConcMarkSweepGC and PrintGCDetails caused startup failures on the new JDK, and the surviving pods ran with -Xmn that defeated G1 adaptivity (illustrative).
